title: The Type System
description: TypeScript's core — annotating values, understanding inference, and thinking in types.

challenges.title: What does a type annotation do?
challenges.description:
You write this in TypeScript:

  let score: number = 100

What does the `: number` part do?
challenges.whyMatters: Understanding what an annotation actually is — a contract, not a cast — is the foundation everything else builds on.
hints: An annotation tells TypeScript what type a value is — it doesn't change the value at runtime.

choices.label: Converts the value to a number at runtime
Tells TypeScript what type the value is, so it can warn you if you use it wrong
Has no effect — TypeScript ignores it

challenges.title: Annotate three variables
challenges.description:
Annotate each variable with the correct type.

Do not change the values — only add the type annotations.

  let username        = "alice"
  let requestCount    = 0
  let isAuthenticated = false
challenges.whyMatters: Explicit annotations on variables make intent clear and catch accidental reassignments early.
hints: The three primitive types in TypeScript are: string, number, boolean
Syntax: let name: string = "value"

challenges.title: Annotate a function
challenges.description:
Write a function `formatPort` that accepts a port number and returns a string in the format `:8080`.

Annotate the parameter and return type explicitly.
challenges.whyMatters: Annotating functions is the most common TypeScript task — it documents the contract and catches callers passing wrong types.
hints: Parameter annotation: (port: number)
Return type goes after the closing paren: ): string
Embed the port directly in a template literal — the output format requires a colon character immediately before the number

challenges.title: Union type parameter
challenges.description:
Write a function `formatId` that accepts an id which can be either a string or a number, and always returns a string.

  formatId(42)      → "42"
  formatId("abc")   → "abc"
challenges.whyMatters: IDs, config values, and API responses often arrive as string or number depending on the source. Union types model this exactly.
hints: Parameter type: id: string | number
String() converts any primitive to a string

challenges.title: Narrow with typeof
challenges.description:
Write a function `stringify` that accepts `string | number | boolean` and always returns a string.

- If it's a string, return it as-is
- If it's a number, return it with 2 decimal places (3 → "3.00")
- If it's a boolean, return "yes" or "no"
challenges.whyMatters: Narrowing with typeof is how you safely handle values from external sources that could be multiple types.
hints: Use typeof to check each case: typeof value === "string"
toFixed(2) works on numbers
Use if / else if / else

challenges.title: Literal return type
challenges.description:
Write a function `getDirection` that takes a number of degrees (0-359) and returns the compass direction as a literal type.

  0-89   → "north"
  90-179 → "east"
  180-269 → "south"
  270-359 → "west"

The return type must be the union: "north" | "east" | "south" | "west"
challenges.whyMatters: Literal types make impossible states impossible — callers know exactly what values to expect, no magic strings.
hints: Return type: ): "north" | "east" | "south" | "west"
Use if / else if chains for the degree ranges
Add a fallback return at the end to satisfy TypeScript

challenges.title: Optional parameter
challenges.description:
Write a function `greet` that takes a name (string) and an optional title (string).

  greet("Alice")           → "Hello, Alice"
  greet("Alice", "Dr.")    → "Hello, Dr. Alice"
challenges.whyMatters: Optional parameters are everywhere in real APIs — understanding how TypeScript handles them prevents a whole class of runtime errors.
hints: The function body is a single conditional — when title is provided use one string format, when it is absent use the other
Check if title is defined before using it
When title is present, insert it with a trailing space before name; when absent nothing should appear — handle both cases inside the template literal

challenges.title: Handle unknown safely
challenges.description:
Write a function `safeLength` that accepts a value of type `unknown` and returns its length as a number.

  safeLength("hello")   → 5
  safeLength([1,2,3])   → 3
  safeLength(42)        → 0  (not a string or array — return 0)
challenges.whyMatters: unknown is the safe alternative to any when handling data from external sources like APIs, JSON, or user input.
hints: typeof value === "string" narrows to string
Array.isArray(value) narrows to array
Return 0 as the fallback

challenges.title: Bring it together
challenges.description:
Write a function `describeValue` that accepts `unknown` and returns a description string.

  describeValue("hello")   → "string of length 5"
  describeValue(42)        → "number: 42"
  describeValue(true)      → "boolean: true"
  describeValue([1,2])     → "array of length 2"
  describeValue({})        → "object"
challenges.whyMatters: This pattern appears in loggers, debuggers, and serializers — anywhere you need to inspect a value you don't control.
hints: Check Array.isArray first — arrays are also typeof "object"
typeof null === "object" — handle that if needed
typeof null === "object" — null is not included in the test cases for this challenge, so no null check is required
